nameStory: Common silverweed gets its shimmering name from the silvery-white undersides of its leaves, which flash like tiny mirrors when stirred by the wind. The silky hairs covering the leaf bottoms create this metallic gleam that makes the plant easy to spot from a distance, especially on sunny days.
description: Common silverweed is a low-growing perennial that spreads along the ground with long, creeping runners called stolons. Its most striking feature is its feathery, compound leaves that are green on top but covered in silky silver hairs underneath. The plant produces cheerful yellow flowers with five rounded petals throughout the summer, sitting on stems that rise just a few inches above the sprawling foliage.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery compound leaves with 7-25 toothed leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stem, dark green above but covered in silky silver hairs beneath that feel soft to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with five rounded petals and a typical rose family center with many stamens, about 3/4 inch across, blooming from late spring through summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Spreads by long, red-tinged runners (stolons) that creep along the ground and root at nodes, forming loose mats rather than growing upright

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel distinctly soft and velvety on the underside due to dense silky hairs, while the top surface is smooth and darker green

habitat: Look for common silverweed in moist, open areas like riverbanks, lakeshores, wet meadows, and roadside ditches throughout New England. It thrives in sandy or gravelly soils that stay consistently moist, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other water-loving plants in areas that may flood seasonally.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their distinctive silver undersides clearly visible, and early flowers may begin appearing by late spring in warmer areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright yellow flowers most abundant, and runners actively spreading to form new plants throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue sporadically into early fall, and the silvery leaf undersides remain prominent even as some foliage begins to fade.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back to the ground, leaving only the root system and dormant growing points to survive until spring.

funFact: Despite being in the rose family, silverweed was historically eaten as a survival food - the starchy roots can be roasted and taste somewhat like sweet potatoes, earning it the nickname 'wild potato' in some regions.
confusionNotes: The silvery leaf undersides make this plant quite distinctive, but beginners might confuse it with other rose family members like wild strawberry or cinquefoils. Remember: silverweed has many more leaflets (7-25 vs 3-5) and that unmistakable silvery shine beneath the leaves.
contextualKnowledge: This plant was formerly classified in the genus Potentilla and may still be listed as Potentilla anserina in older field guides. The name 'cinquefoil' traditionally refers to five-leaflet plants, so 'silver cinquefoil' is somewhat misleading since silverweed typically has many more than five leaflets.
compareHints: Common silverweed is the only member of the Argentina genus in New England, making it unique among local rose family members for its many-leafleted compound leaves with silvery undersides. Other rose family plants in the region either have simple three-part leaves (like strawberries) or five-fingered leaves (like true cinquefoils), but none have silverweed's distinctive feathery appearance and metallic sheen.
